name: APT28
summary: APT28 is a threat group that has been attributed to Russia's General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU) 85th Main Special Service Center (GTsSS) military unit 26165. This group has been active since at least 2004. APT28 reportedly compromised the Hillary Clinton campaign, the Democratic National Committee, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2016 in an attempt to interfere with the U.S. presidential election. In 2018, the US indicted five GRU Unit 26165 officers associated with APT28 for cyber operations (including close-access operations) conducted between 2014 and 2018 against the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), the US Anti-Doping Agency, a US nuclear facility, the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), the Spiez Swiss Chemicals Laboratory, and other organizations.

procedures.text: APT28 has used a UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) rootkit known as LoJax.
APT28 encrypted a.dll payload using RTL and a custom encryption algorithm. APT28 has also obfuscated payloads with base64, XOR, and RC4.
APT28 has renamed the WinRAR utility to avoid detection.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 has changed extensions on files containing exfiltrated data to make them appear benign, and renamed a web shell instance to appear as a legitimate OWA page.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 has intentionally deleted computer files to cover their tracks, including with use of the program CCleaner.
APT28 has performed timestomping on victim files.

APT28 has used legitimate credentials to gain initial access, maintain access, and exfiltrate data from a victim network. The group has specifically used credentials stolen through a spearphishing email to login to the DCCC network.
APT28 has used compromised Office 365 service accounts with Global Administrator privileges to collect email from user inboxes.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 has used CVE-2015-1701 to access the SYSTEM token and copy it into the current process as part of privilege escalation.
An APT28 macro uses the command `certutil -decode` to decode contents of a.txt file storing the base64 encoded payload.
APT28 has used CVE-2015-4902 to bypass security features.

APT28 executed CHOPSTICK by using rundll32 commands such as `rundll32.exe “C:\Windows\twain_64.dll”`. APT28 also executed a.dll for a first stage dropper using rundll32.exe. An APT28 loader Trojan saved a batch script that uses rundll32 to execute a DLL payload.
APT28 used weaponized Microsoft Word documents abusing the remote template function to retrieve a malicious macro.
APT28 has deployed a bootkit along with Downdelph to ensure its persistence on the victim. The bootkit shares code with some variants of BlackEnergy.
APT28 has saved files with hidden file attributes.
APT28 has used the WindowStyle parameter to conceal PowerShell windows.
LAMEHUG has sent spearphishing emails impersonating Ukrainian government officials.
APT28 has cleared event logs, including by using the commands `wevtutil cl System` and `wevtutil cl Security`.
APT28 has harvested user's login credentials.
APT28 has used large language models (LLMs) to gather information about satellite capabilities.
APT28 has performed large-scale scans in an attempt to find vulnerable servers.
APT28 has used large language models (LLMs) to assist in script development and deployment.
APT28 has used spearphishing to compromise credentials.

procedures.text: APT28 has obtained and used open-source tools like Koadic, Mimikatz, and Responder.
APT28 has deployed LAMEHUG which can can query an LLM to generate and return commands for post compromise activity on targeted systems.
APT28 uses a tool to infect connected USB devices and transmit itself to air-gapped computers when the infected USB device is inserted.
APT28 has used Tor and a variety of commercial VPN services to route brute force authentication attempts.

procedures.text: APT28 has compromised targets via strategic web compromise utilizing custom exploit kits. APT28 used reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) against government websites to redirect users to phishing webpages.

APT28 has exploited open Wi-Fi access points for initial access to target devices using the network.
APT28 downloads and executes PowerShell scripts and performs PowerShell commands.

APT28 has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerability CVE-2017-0262 for execution.
APT28 has tricked unwitting recipients into clicking on malicious hyperlinks within emails crafted to resemble trustworthy senders.

An APT28 loader Trojan adds the Registry key `HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript` to establish persistence.

APT28 has used a modified and obfuscated version of the reGeorg web shell to maintain persistence on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server.

procedures.text: APT28 has used COM hijacking for persistence by replacing the legitimate `MMDeviceEnumerator` object with a payload.
APT28 has deployed malware that has copied itself to the startup directory for persistence.
APT28 has exploited CVE-2014-4076, CVE-2015-2387, CVE-2015-1701, CVE-2017-0263, and CVE-2022-38028 to escalate privileges.
APT28 regularly deploys both publicly available (ex: Mimikatz) and custom password retrieval tools on victims.

procedures.text: APT28 has used the ntdsutil.exe utility to export the Active Directory database for credential access.

procedures.text: APT28 deployed the open source tool Responder to conduct NetBIOS Name Service poisoning, which captured usernames and hashed passwords that allowed access to legitimate credentials. APT28 close-access teams have used Wi-Fi pineapples to intercept Wi-Fi signals and user credentials.

procedures.text: APT28 has used tools to perform keylogging.
APT28 can perform brute force attacks to obtain credentials.

APT28 has used a brute-force/password-spray tooling that operated in two modes: in brute-force mode it typically sent over 300 authentication attempts per hour per targeted account over the course of several hours or days. APT28 has also used a Kubernetes cluster to conduct distributed, large-scale password guessing attacks.

procedures.text: APT28 has used several malicious applications to steal user OAuth access tokens including applications masquerading as "Google Defender" "Google Email Protection," and "Google Scanner" for Gmail users. They also targeted Yahoo users with applications masquerading as "Delivery Service" and "McAfee Email Protection".
APT28 has used a Wi-Fi Pineapple to set up Evil Twin Wi-Fi Poisoning for the purposes of capturing victim credentials or planting espionage-oriented malware.

procedures.text: An APT28 loader Trojan will enumerate the victim's processes searching for explorer.exe if its current process does not have necessary permissions.
APT28 has used Forfiles to locate PDF, Excel, and Word documents during collection. The group also searched a compromised DCCC computer for specific terms.
APT28 uses a module to receive a notification every time a USB mass storage device is inserted into a victim.
APT28 has mapped network drives using Net and administrator credentials.

APT28 has used several malicious applications that abused OAuth access tokens to gain access to target email accounts, including Gmail and Yahoo Mail.
APT28 has used pass the hash for lateral movement.
APT28 has retrieved internal documents from machines inside victim environments, including by using Forfiles to stage documents before exfiltration.
An APT28 backdoor may collect the entire contents of an inserted USB device.
APT28 has collected files from network shared drives.

APT28 has staged archives of collected data on a target's Outlook Web Access (OWA) server.

APT28 has collected files from various information repositories.

APT28 used a publicly available tool to gather and compress multiple documents on the DCCC and DNC networks.
APT28 has used a variety of utilities, including WinRAR, to archive collected data with password protection.

procedures.text: APT28 added "junk data" to each encoded string, preventing trivial decoding without knowledge of the junk removal algorithm. Each implant was given a "junk length" value when created, tracked by the controller software to allow seamless communication but prevent analysis of the command protocol on the wire.
Later implants used by APT28, such as CHOPSTICK, use a blend of HTTP, HTTPS, and other legitimate channels for C2, depending on module configuration.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 has used IMAP, POP3, and SMTP for a communication channel in various implants, including using self-registered Google Mail accounts and later compromised email servers of its victims.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 used other victims as proxies to relay command traffic, for instance using a compromised Georgian military email server as a hop point to NATO victims. The group has also used a tool that acts as a proxy to allow C2 even if the victim is behind a router.
APT28 has routed traffic over Tor and VPN servers to obfuscate their activities.
APT28 uses a tool that captures information from air-gapped computers via an infected USB and transfers it to network-connected computer when the USB is inserted.
APT28 has used Google Drive for C2.
APT28 has downloaded additional files, including by using a first-stage downloader to contact the C2 server to obtain the second-stage implant.
APT28 installed a Delphi backdoor that used a custom algorithm for C2 communications.
APT28 has split archived exfiltration files into chunks smaller than 1MB.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 has exfiltrated archives of collected data previously staged on a target's OWA server via HTTPS.

cites.name: Cybersecurity Advisory GRU Brute Force Campaign July 2021

procedures.text: APT28 can exfiltrate data over Google Drive.
In 2016, APT28 conducted a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack against the World Anti-Doping Agency.
